newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan keeping closer tabs on forex market - traders.
newsitem.headline: Japan keeping closer tabs on forex market - traders.

text.p: Japanese monetary authorities have stepped up their efforts to keep currencies under control by keeping in close touch with influential market participants, market sources said on Tuesday.
The dollar/yen rate has apparently been tamed by remarks from government officials after recent volatile movements.
But traders said the stability is not only due to those public remarks but Japanese officials' efforts behind the scenes to let market participants know of their intentions.
"(The authorities) appear to have made various efforts to stabilise the currency market," said one fund manager.
He said, for instance, that members of the Finance Ministry's foreign exchange division invited influential market operators to meet informally to exchange views on the markets.
The authorities also took pains to collect detailed activities of investors and exporters through Japanese and foreign banks in Tokyo, he said.

In return for market information, the authorities would interpret the meaning behind the comments made by the finance minister and other officials on currencies, traders said. They would also signal a direction for the dollar/yen, they said.
A fund manager at a major institutional investor said: "We often get phone calls from (MOF) suggesting the right timing to buy (dollars)".

A senior ministry of finance official said that MOF would never pressure investors to buy or sell dollars, although they do maintain contact with market participants on a daily basis for the purpose of exchanging information.
But the talk in the market was that the bureaucrats urged major Japanese life insurance firms to bargain-hunt for the dollar when it tumbled as low as 111.98 yen last week.
On Tuesday, the dollar rose as high as 116.69 yen in Tokyo.
After hitting a May 1 peak of 127.47 yen, it then fell sharply on May 8 on a remark by senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that the dollar could fall to 103 yen.
The dollar tumble stopped again after Sakakibara and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka's comments last week that a correction against excessive yen falls was over.

Tokyo dealers believe that Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for his influence on currency markets, is also in close touch with overseas hedge funds and Asian central banks -- major market players which can sometimes set the trade's direction.
"What (the ministry) is trying to do is to put influential operators on their side by establishing a close relationship," said the first fund manager.
Indeed, traders said it was difficult to trade the dollar beyond the range that the authorities felt comfortable in.
"It seems to be impossible to push the dollar out of a 110-120 yen range for now, since they appear content with a dollar/yen rate of 115 yen," said a senior Tokyo bank trader.
One analyst said that there may be problems with providing a limited number of participants with beneficial information.

But he added that monetary authorities having contact with a wider range of participants is important for them to be admitted into the market as one of the participants and to wield influence once the dollar deviates largely from fundamentals.

Analysts and government officials agree that a stable dollar/yen exchange rate is vital for Japan to keep its economy on the recovery track and to avoid a renewed rise in trade friction with the United States.
